analysis.one_liner: Writes a Clean Water Act definition of "fill material" that would stop coal companies from dumping mining waste into Appalachian streams.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar dumping coal mining waste into streams was referred to the Senate environment committee in March 2009 and never advanced further before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Water Act to define "fill material" as anything that replaces water with dry land or raises the bottom of a body of water, while specifically excluding the dumping of excess spoil from coal surface mining into waters of the United States [S2][S3]. The practical effect, according to the bill's stated purpose, is to stop coal companies from pushing mountaintop-removal mining waste into valleys and streams, a practice currently permitted under the existing definition of fill material [S1]. The bill never got past the referral stage: it was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream of Appalachian surface mines — those whose streams, drinking water, and flood-prone valleys are affected by mining waste being dumped into headwater streams. The bill would permanently bar that practice by writing it into the Clean Water Act, and its bipartisan sponsorship included a Tennessee senator whose state's mountains are affected by mountaintop removal [S1][S2][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Appalachian communities near mountaintop removal mines

how_it_helps.text: It defines 'fill material' under the Clean Water Act so that mining spoil dumped into streams to create dry land or raise a streambed can no longer be permitted as fill, effectively barring the dumping of excess coal mining spoil in waters of the United States.
Because the exclusion is written into the Clean Water Act itself, the protection would not depend on agency rules that future administrations could weaken.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies engaged in surface mining in Appalachia, which would lose the ability to dispose of excess mining spoil in valleys and streams, and potentially coal-mining communities where that disposal method lowers mining costs and supports jobs.

drawbacks.text: The bill's restriction would make it far harder or impossible to dispose of mining spoil in valleys, which could sharply curtail surface mining in Appalachia and cost jobs in coal-dependent communities.

The new definition of fill material covers any pollutant that replaces water with dry land or raises a water body's bottom 'for any purpose,' a broad sweep that goes well beyond mining and could create permitting uncertainty for other construction and disposal activities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanent, statutory protection for Appalachian headwater streams from being buried by mining waste — is significant and would have been durable, since it would write the definition into law rather than leave it to agency rules that can change with administrations. The cost is real: ending valley fills would sharply curtail a mining method that supports jobs in parts of Appalachia with few alternatives, and the coal industry argued the change would raise electricity costs and eliminate mining employment. A fair weighing comes down to whether the ecological and drinking-water harm of valley fills outweighs those economic losses; the bill's sponsors said the science on stream destruction justified the restriction [S1][S2]. It is a blunt instrument, but its purpose was narrow and clear.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Environment and Public Works Committee in March 2009, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended, so it died with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 25, 2009 and read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
That referral was the last action of any kind in the bill's history; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the 111th Congress.
When the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, the bill was dead; it was not carried over to the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies that dump mining waste into valleys and streams are better off, because the practice stays permitted under the existing Clean Water Act rules the bill would have changed.

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
for.what_they_did: Joined Cardin in introducing the bill as an original cosponsor.

for.name: 9 of 58 Senate Democrats, 1 of 40 Senate Republicans, and the Senate's 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, 11 senators in total, in a coalition that crossed party lines.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report — through the end of the 111th Congress.

against.name: Coal mining industry
against.role: Coal operators and industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on dumping mining spoil into valleys and streams, which the bill would have effectively barred for surface mining operations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors spanned both parties — a Democratic sponsor from Maryland, a Republican original cosponsor from Tennessee, and 11 cosponsors including 9 of 58 Senate Democrats, 1 of 40 Senate Republicans, and the chamber's 1 Independent [S4] — but it never progressed far enough for a party-line floor fight.

industries.industry: Coal mining (surface mining and mountaintop removal operators)
industries.note: The bill would prohibit the industry's standard practice of dumping excess mining spoil into valleys and streams, a method central to mountaintop removal mining in Appalachia. The bill died without a vote, so the industry kept the existing regime.
Restricting mountaintop removal could raise coal supply costs for utilities and ratepayers in coal-dependent regions. Because the bill never advanced, nothing changed.

industries.industry: Downstream water users and Appalachian communities
industries.note: Not an industry, but the communities whose streams and drinking water sources sit below valley fills are the intended beneficiaries; burying headwater streams under mining spoil is associated with degraded water quality and flooding. They gained nothing because the bill never moved.
